articles.title: Wabi, the AI agent that builds mini apps, now valued at $1.25B after latest round
articles.reason: 涵盖 AI product & news、AI agent & application
articles.summary: On Thursday, AI app Wabi, now describing itself as a "personal agent," said it has raised $55 million at a $1.25 billion valuation.
articles.full_text:
The race to build the winning AI assistant is on, and investors are spreading out their bets.

On Thursday, another AI app, Wabi , now describing itself as a “personal agent,” said it has raised $55 million at a $1.25 billion valuation.

Founded by Eugenia Kuyda, who previously founded the AI companion startup Replika, Wabi originally focused on allowing anyone to build apps using prompts .

Last month, however, the startup announced a pivot of sorts to become an AI messenger.

The idea now is that the new Wabi — or Wabi 2.0, as it was called — could build the interfaces you need to get things done as part of its role as your personal AI agent.

The company suggests Wabi could be used to build mini apps for things like meal planning, tracking local restaurants, planning date nights, creating fitness plans, designing specialized trivia games, and more.

The additional funding indicates that Wabi’s investors agree that its new agentic angle has some potential, especially given the market around AI agents is hot right now, with viral AI agent Instinct pulling in another billion at a $10 billion valuation in September.

Even Tolan, which makes a cute, Muppet-like AI companion to help people navigate life, just raised $30 million . “Eugenia has a unique sense for where AI is headed and a track record of great taste in building it,” said Alex Lim, general partner at IVP, which led the new round, in a statement. “She has a clear vision for how people will interact with AI, one that goes far beyond the text box or command line.

Wabi is the expression of that vision, and we’re thrilled to support her.” Other participants in the round included Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), Forerunner, Amazon Alexa Fund, and angel investors like Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke, Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff, former Yahoo! head Marissa Mayer, former Twitter CEO Dick Costolo, and one half of The Chainsmokers, Alex Pall.

articles.full_text:
Podcasts AI Business Anthropic is asking Wall Street to believe in AGI SemiAnalysis’ Joey Brookhart helps break down the Anthropic S-1 and why he thinks the company could be worth $10 trillion. by Nilay Patel Oct 29, 2026, 2:00 PM UTC Link Share Nilay Patel is editor-in-chief of The Verge, host of the Decoder podcast , and co-host of The Vergecast .

Today on Decoder , I’m joined by Joey Brookhart, an analyst at the chip and AI research firm SemiAnalysis, to help me dig into the story inside the numbers of the Anthropic IPO filing — a document known as an S-1.

Anthropic just filed its S-1 to go public on the Nasdaq, and it could start trading as soon as next month at a valuation of anywhere between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion.

That would immediately make it one of the most valuable companies on the planet.

But the price tag really isn’t the whole story here.

The S-1 document published earlier this week is hundreds upon hundreds of pages filled with details that finally paint a picture of the economics of a frontier AI lab.

As you might imagine, that picture is both really complicated and built on a series of very, very ambitious assumptions about the future and what AI will do to it .

So I wanted to have Joey on the show to help break down what this document tells us, both about Anthropic’s finances and the broader AI economy.

Joey and his colleagues at SemiAnalysis actually built a model of Anthropic’s finances from the outside back in July, so he’s been waiting for this filing about as eagerly as anyone, and I was excited to hear his take on what we’ve learned and, importantly, what we still don’t know.

Okay: SemiAnalysis’ Joey Brookhart on the Anthropic S-1 and the costs and risks of building frontier AI.

Here we go.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Joey Brookhart, you are an analyst at SemiAnalysis.

You’re also co-lead on SemiAnalysis’ Tokenomics model, which is going to come up a lot in this episode.

Welcome to Decoder .

Yeah, thanks so much, Nilay.

I am very excited to talk to you.

We’re talking just a couple days after the big Anthropic S-1 was filed.

It’s our first look inside of the finances of one of the leading frontier models.

What’s your take?

What’s your read into it?

It was an awesome S-1.

It’s been a rough three weeks since the investor day.

Some people were somewhat disappointed in the September [annualized recurring revenue] numbers, but what we saw here was a company that has efficiently scaled to an amazing level, with a $1 trillion-plus valuation, $70 billion-plus of ARR in a very short amount of time.

In gross margins, compute margins, and free cash flow, everything is what you’d want to see.

So I don’t think there was much to nitpick in this filing.

It’s the reason you’ve seen a lot of the semiconductor complex, and the neoclouds and compute stocks, really rally again in the last two days.

It’s funny, I don’t think I can nitpick the S-1 itself.

I want to get into some of the details because there are a lot of numbers in there that are worth thinking about.

I actually just want to start at the really big picture.

You run a thing called Tokenomics.

I’m going to explain what Tokenomics is to people.

I look at Anthropic and where it could go.

I look at Dario Amodei saying that he can see his way to $1 trillion in revenue.

Where does that money come from?

Because so much of these businesses are about eating every other business and it feels like someone else has to make some money to pay Anthropic to generate these revenues.

I haven’t actually seen that laid out very clearly.

Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts.

Head here .

Not a subscriber?

You can sign up here .

It’s so interesting.

Today, because even the scale we’re at is $120 billion of ARR between the two leading labs, it’s still an extremely narrow market.

The top 1 percent of customers are the ones that are spending $50,000 to $100,000 per employee.

Your broader Fortune 500 or Global 2000, which typically do a lot of IT spend, isn’t spending much.

A lot of the spending, especially at Anthropic, is coding-specific.

It’s almost a single vertical company.

We look in the future to 2027, you think to this broader adoption and white collar work.

This typical enterprise Q4 budgeting season, we actually haven’t gone through with one of these labs yet in any meaningful way because their ARR did really start to accelerate until the beginning of the year.

We think of other cases like cyber, which can be similar to coding, where these are eight-figure-plus contracts with leading enterprises that can scale very quickly due to all the cybersecurity incidents we’re seeing.

You get to other verticals like bio.

To get to $1 trillion, we do have to move to some of that white collar work, where it goes from AI augmentation to labor saving or replacement in some areas.

You look at things like Microsoft’s buyout offers to employees as an example of this , but there’s no wealth of other verticals that they can get into and really start to move the needle.

This is the single biggest question I have, not just about the S-1, but the entire industry.

I would understand that if there are one or two leading labs.

There are two big companies that have a technology that can automate a whole bunch of things.

We will see how well that automation goes sector by sector, but there are not just two leading labs.

There are quite a few of them.

There are open weight models.

I’ve heard from a lot of CEOs who are very nervous about giving all their data to an OpenAI or Anthropic and they would like to run some things on-prem.

There are law firms running on-prem AI now, which is the funniest turn in maybe all of history.

How do you see that playing out?

Because so much of the pressure on this S-1 was the numbers themselves, which I want to talk about, but then there’s the external pressure of, “You’ve got to grow and growth is not as short.” So how do you see all of that playing out?

It’s very interesting because when we look at coding today, for example — and I think we saw this in Q3 with OpenAI kind of catching up — there are areas of coding where there are very low switching costs, and I can just move between that.

What we hear from enterprises and maybe, too, on the OpenAI side — obviously I think they somewhat botched the Fable release, and the lack of zero data retention is why we saw some of the slowdown.

That’s something they can fix with Fable 5.5 and maybe drive more enterprise adoption there.

That’s a huge thing for enterprises when we talk with them.

We definitely see enterprises now, and more so, too, a lot of the AI natives, doing custom training and post-training on open weight models, and then running either their inference off of that or even their products for internal or external use cases.

Obviously, DeepMind at Google and [Meta Superintelligence Labs] are very well-funded labs that have pretty similar training compute capacity, and they’re bringing on a ton of it.

Not even to mention SpaceX as well, with what Elon said on [about] 10 net new gigawatts next year and half of that is the long-term internal use case.

In the first half of the year, Anthropic ran away with it.

They were 90 percent of the industry’s net new ARR.

We saw in Q3 that OpenAI was probably actually the majority of industry net new ARR.

Open-source has grown from probably $1 billion of token inference costs, ARR, in Q1 to $10 billion-plus here in Q3.

So yes, the industry’s gotten much more competitive, but there are all these new use cases, too, and some of these verticalized use cases are really where we’re going to see the growth going forward.

Because it’s obvious coding isn’t going to power us to even triple from here.

It’s interesting.

The concept is called Tokenomics.

You run that practice alongside another co-lead at SemiAnalysis.

Explain what it is because to me it’s such a smart way of thinking about, “We’re going to put some money in and maybe we’ll get some money out.” I think of it as the unit economics [of AI], or even just the broader idea — everything from a macro- to microeconomics of running an AI business or even looking at AI demand.

So we cover the hyperscalers, now some of the neoclouds as well in a separate product.

But then just the AI labs, too.

For investors, or just people that are interested in the business, Anthropic had negative 94 percent gross margins on inference two years ago.

Now they have a positive 85 percent margin, and people don’t understand how they allocate compute.

How do we think about the inference business model?

Part of that gross margin conversation is the revenue per megawatt in inference.

Why are all companies that are running inference seeing massive gains in inference and compute efficiency?

So we try to model out these businesses and obviously when Anthropic was private, we’re dealing with information we can get from the press and things like that.

But now that we have concrete audited numbers, it’s easy to explain the unit economics of this.

And also how the businesses differ.

OpenAI is a much different business than Anthropic just in both their consumption versus subscription and then historical weight versus consumer versus enterprise. [We are] trying to understand across the demand level the economics of these businesses.

Several years ago when I talked to Google CEO Sundar Pichai about the cost of inference, I said, “How are you ever going to make money?” He was just very clear.

He said, “If there’s one thing Google’s good at, it’s bringing this stuff down the cost curve.” It was a very blunt answer.

I understand how Google can do it.

They make their own chips.

Anthropic is running on everyone else’s clouds.

The core part of the S-1 is how much they’ve committed to spend on other people’s clouds: SpaceXAI, Google, Amazon.

Where does their efficiency come from?

There’s really token throughput.

They have a very diverse chip fleet.

Between Trainiums, TPUs, and GPUs, across all of those, we see a ton of token efficiencies.

Token throughput, for example, on Trainium chips is up 5x to 10x year-over-year right now.

Dealing with both the hardware level efficiencies and the software — and how the model interacts with the hardware — there are a lot of token throughput gains where if you’re doing X tokens per second, now you’re doing five or 10 times that just a year later.

What they’ll tell you is they see continued compute efficiencies as well going forward.

Max Kan, who co-leads Tokenomics model with me at SemiAnalysis, and I have even published some research on this.

Right now, if Anthropic’s at $65 million of revenue per inference megawatt, this was mid-teens last year at this time.

What we’ve said on maybe Opus 5.5 on a [Nvidia] Blackwell, you can get to $100 to $120 million of revenue per megawatt.

The big thing here is they’re paying on average now just a little over $10 million per megawatt in [cost of goods sold], or just in compute costs.

What you can do with those margins is then reinvest in training.

People don’t realize this, but only about 30 percent of the compute is actually in inference-serving revenue.

The rest is for experimentation and research, training models, and post-training models.

So there’s a lot of compute that is building the next model and that’s more of the R&D side and where you actually get your returns and defensibility in this business.

Actually, what I was expecting to see in the S-1 was that dynamic play out much more strongly — that Anthropic makes a bunch of money selling the models they have now and there are more customers in the future for the models they have now.

That’s going to throw off a whole bunch of margin.

And then, because it is Anthropic and they think they’re building a digital god, they’re going to train the next models as much as they can.

That is a very particular Anthropic story.

The company is chasing AGI.

The people who work there will happily tell you that in the S-1 that Claude might be conscious and this could all go to hell.

Anthropic is a very unique company in its conception of itself.

But you don’t really see that dynamic playing out in the S-1.

They’re managing their training costs against their inference margin pretty well.

Do you see that going up or changing in any way?

I agree.

Long term, and we’ve even said this internally, they want to actually increase the percentage of training.

If you believe you’re building a digital god or going towards AGI, and as long as you have the gross margins of 85 percent-plus on inference to do so, you can.

They’ve grown a lot faster than they thought, and they didn’t expect to be at 11 percent non-gap EBITA margins.

They’d love to be closer to zero, or even below that if they could get that compute and allocate it towards training and continue to see these compute efficiencies.

They’ve messaged that, too, to investors in the roadshow.

You can look at this S-1 and just the curve of profitability over the last few years and how little cash they burned to get to this point and you can say, “This is a good business model, but we’re going towards AGI.

Don’t expect the margin leverage we’re seeing to continue to this level, even though long-term margins can be quite a bit higher.” There are some real shades of Amazon there.

Jeff Bezos famously told investors he wasn’t going to make money until he could make a lot of money.

Obviously, Amazon and Anthropic have a lot of back and forth.

Maybe there’s some family resemblance there.

But I’m curious, there’s a point of model capability that would allow you to go into more verticals than just coding, right?

We might be at it now.

The idea of capability overhang exists, the idea that the models we have today could go and take over bio research.

They’re taking over mathematics today.

There’s a point at which the smartest business decision is to stop training and to just sell your profitable model into more and more companies.

Anthropic as a public company will face that pressure.

Do you think they’re organized or structured to fend it off?

Yeah, I think they’re structured well.

With some of the voting stock in areas like that, they definitely are.

We’ve seen this in tech before and even publicly when Mark Zuckerberg has made these decisions before to invest heavily.

It didn’t always pay off.

I just want to point out, it didn’t always pay off.

Yeah, it did not always pay off.

Although you and I technically are in the metaverse right now, by some definition. [Laughs] Right.

But I think that’s something, and there’s an interesting number in the S-1 that 80 percent of revenue in the last three months comes from models released in the last six months.

So then you say, “Okay, 20 percent of the models are like Opus 4.5 in earlier versions.” One thing going forward is that if you’re a frontier model company, you always need to be at the frontier and it’s incredibly competitive.

Wait, can I ask a really dumb question about that?

Yeah.

Why?

I think the heart of my curiosity about the industry right now is if you enabled some bleeding-edge technology that could revolutionize the entire world, at some point, the most profitable thing to do is to just go play it out in all the different verticals, right?

It’s not to go make the next one.

It’s actually to run an efficient model in legal services and medicine and wherever else that there hasn’t been diffusion of AI yet.

This idea that you always have to be at the frontier, that Anthropic always has to be competing with Google and OpenAI and whoever else, I get it from their self-conception.

But from a business point of view, an AI-enabled business is going to throw out more money and spend more money with me, the AI provider, and that isn’t necessarily related to being at the frontier.

There are a few portions of that.

For new verticals, and this is very cyber specific, if an adversary is using a frontier model, you need to be defending with a frontier model.

Fair enough.

When we talk to some enterprises, it’s not like an email summary where I can run that on open source or Sonnet.

There are just certain verticals where having... [For example,] if you were in a legal case as a defendant, would you be okay if your lawyer was using a non-frontier model if the prosecution— [Laughs] I got bad news for you about what’s going on in the legal market right now.

The competitive dynamics do dictate that.

I think from a go-forward perspective, we’ve seen this with open source too catching up in one point, but the demand will be there. [SemiAnalysis CEO] Dylan [Patel] says this a lot.

The demand will always be there for frontier intelligence, especially in competitive industries.

And there are certain tasks, as you go towards more labor replacement versus labor augmentation, where that also is the case.

At the same time, they are getting more vertical.

If you go look at job postings or what they’re hiring for, they’re putting out more of these SKUs and areas, and there’s a lot of beta testing going on like Claude for financial services, Claude for legal, their cyber program.

They’re giving away 25,000 of credits per month for people in their cyber program.

That’ll be a huge SKU for them in 2027.

Those verticalized areas and then ones that are specifically where you need to be...

It’s more adversarial, I should say, or competitive, are the main reasons why.

But we can both agree there are areas like email summary and work that definitely doesn’t need to happen [at the frontier].

I’ll just make a dumb comparison to the iPhone.

It’s iPhone season.

I just reviewed the iPhone Duo.

Apple kept the iPhone looking the same for several years now.

They build all of the tooling for the new iPhone and then they just reuse it for two or three or four models to get all the value out of that investment back before they move on to the next thing.

Apple puts out a new iPhone, and it keeps selling the old iPhone for a while to get more value out of that investment and that development program.

The AI industry does not seem to be doing that.

All of their emphasis is on developing the next new thing, deprecating the old thing pretty fast, and moving you onto the new expensive product, while at the same time they’re building the next new expensive product.

At some point it feels like that will rationalize, that there will be something that is worth just collecting margin from while they go invest in the new thing.

I just can’t figure out where Anthropic sits in that cycle.

I mean, we do see this.

Open source token volumes are picking up and there’s a lot of areas, yes, where the open source models have become good enough.

I think on a go-forward basis, you’re like, “Okay, was that because of distillation?” And then the frontier labs have some defensibility actually going forward.

I think when we talk to clients, it’s also about how we actually think about frontier versus open source.

So something like a Sonnet type model, if you want to do the iPhone 18 versus the SE type analogy.

We do see that dynamic, and obviously with open source, it’s a question of how much that can take.

Two, because we’re so early in these verticals, we don’t know what’s going to be fully agentic.

There’s no human in the loop where the harness actually has, I should say, some value and defensibility to it.

The big area I’d look at here, especially when we talk to enterprises today, is only the coders are allowed to use the frontier models at a lot of these enterprises.

If you’re a non-coder, some of these companies just limit you to Sonnet, if you’re an Anthropic customer.

That’s reflective of how management views and wants to budget for this, what frontier intelligence is actually worth to them in certain areas.

In my financial analyst brain, Claude could not build a good financial model six months ago.

It’s getting better if you connect it to the right areas, but we’ve gone from something like, “I needed a junior analyst six months ago,” to, “Maybe I don’t as much anymore,” and then, “Will I have a full junior analyst at my disposal anytime or multiple pretty quickly, if I have unlimited token budget?” We just look at that across every vertical and major job category.

The time horizon in each of those categories is going to be different.

That’s just one of the bigger questions I have: How quickly do they get to where they think they can go?

I want to dig in on some of the numbers here.

The one that jumped out in all of the comment sections on all of the forums and all of our articles yesterday was $80 billion.

Anthropic lost $80 billion [in the first half of 2026].

That is related to a technical charge.

Can you just explain the $80 billion?

Because it doesn’t seem particularly relevant to the revenue and profits they’re talking about.

Yeah, it’s a non-cash charge because their valuation has gone up so much and they’ve issued warrants or convertible notes.

You have to account for that in your balance sheet.

It’s just a non-cash charge because their valuation has gone up so much since they issued these warrants and notes.

That’s something you would always back out.

You can argue on stuff like stock-based compensation.

Should we really be thinking about that on a non-GAAP cash basis?

Because it’s non-cash, if I just hand employees shares, I have to account for that on my income statement, but I’m not actually handing them pure cash out of my bank balance.

So it’s not an area like that.

It gets the accounting, the high level.

If you don’t know accounting, it looks bad, but it’s because they’ve grown so much and their valuation has gone up so much.

Some of the argument here about that charge is that Amazon was the other party there.

Obviously Amazon’s very happy because Anthropic is buying a ton of AWS and sure they’re happy the valuation has gone up, but over time Amazon’s going to get diluted this way.

That’s part of the dynamic there.

Anthropic is going to obviously IPO.

They’re going to put a bunch of shares in the market.

It’s very clear that over time they will issue more shares to raise more money.

It doesn’t seem like they’re going to stop wanting to raise money anytime soon.

How are you thinking about that in terms of just investment into a company like Anthropic, that your valuation might be going up, but your actual ownership stake might be getting diluted over time?

The deals have always been very creatively structured.

The number is they’ve actually only burned $10 billion of cash.

They have $120 billion-plus of cash and marketable securities in the balance sheet today, and post-IPO, probably another $100 billion.

It’s a great deal for both parties.

They only really rent compute.

It’s not like they have these massive capital outlays or even rent-to-own.

You can make some arguments about certain accounting and there are these massive compute commitment obligations and that’s technically future debt, or that is sitting somewhat off balance sheet essentially.

But from a dilution perspective, all tech companies dilute.

Are they going to need to raise another $100 billion of debt or equity at some point?

Possibly.

Can they continue to creatively structure and finance future compute buildouts?

Probably as well.

I know there’s been a lot of angst about the future of compute financing and data center financing in the last few weeks.

But if you’re Anthropic, if you’re a major lab, a hyperscaler or Broadcom or Nvidia that are backstopping a lot of these deals, that’s probably not going to change anytime soon.

So I’m not particularly worried.

As an equity investor, would I be worried about getting super diluted?

I don’t think so.

If you believe in this long-term AGI bull case and that Anthropic is going to be a leader in this, that probably shouldn’t worry you.

You’re probably looking at a $10 trillion-plus business.

They can outrun dilution at that point.

Let’s talk about the compute commitments.

I saw at least one analysis saying over the next 10 years, it’s $800 billion-plus in commitments to the various hyperscalers and neoclouds.

That’s a lot.

You’re saying that they don’t have that much money.

They haven’t even spent that much money yet.

Do you see them generating the revenues to pay off those commitments?

Yeah.

I think when people look at the headline commitments, the $500 to $600 billion number over 7 to 10 years, let’s call it, what they’re paying for compute today actually isn’t that many gigawatts.

If you think about their spending right now, on average they’re close to $11 million per megawatt in spend, or $11 billion per gigawatt.

If you take that back to the annual level and say, “Okay, the $520 billion number is over 70 years, for example, that’s really not that many gigawatts and they’re going to be well beyond…” When they get to something like 20 gigawatts, the future compute commitments that they’re running essentially is going to be well into the trillions.

So yes, they are going to have the revenue to do so.

It’s more about how much revenue they are going to have relative to how much compute.

Two, the compute efficiency equation.

If they keep getting a lot more revenue out of every inference megawatt, how much do you really want to invest in training and take margins to zero from a rental perspective?

Because you can get to something where even 80 percent to 85 percent of their fleet is just on training and research at these kinds of margins.

The revenue is going to scale pretty well.

They’re not in any dire situations there.

Unless we realize all this revenue disappears or people churn.

It’s not like they have to hit a trillion dollars of revenue extremely, extremely quickly to achieve all this and pay for this.

Unless you’re trying to build digital God and unless it doesn’t diffuse across the economy as fast as everyone wants it to.

Those are bets, right?

They’re huge bets.

The numbers you look at, if you’re really bullish on this ramp into the digital economy, is Anthropic saying within their Fortune 500 customers, they have 50 percent of the Fortune 500 and that is just 0.1 percent of their total customers’ operating expenses.

When you look at that on a per user basis, it’s like $8 a month if you believe OpEx doesn’t include the cost of goods sold.

If you believe they include the cost of goods sold, it’s sub-$50 per month.

They said the same thing.

Of the top 5 percent of Claude Code users, they’re spending $18,000 a year on average, the top 5 percent of users.

Their non-Claude Code users spend under $75 a month, well under $75.

There’s this huge opportunity, especially when we talk to enterprises and these traditional buyers of IT software.

Penetration is extremely low in traditional white collar work.

That’s the big point, too, that there is a large ramp period here of both seats adoption and usage.

You can make arguments of who’s going to win in this, but it’s obvious the frontier labs are going to get some portion of this and it’s going to be pretty material to net new ARR next year.

One of the things that’s really interesting about that is we talk about the frontier labs, we talk about the hyperscalers — Anthropic has a lot of wild risk factors in this S-1, including that Claude might be conscious and kill us all.

But one of the most direct and maybe easiest to understand is that AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud are both suppliers and competitors in some real way, particularly Google.

And they say, “These relationships could turn.” They have a big relationship with SpaceXAI.

Elon Musk is going to train Grok.

They’re going to compete with SpaceXAI at some point.

That relationship might become precarious.

As you say, they’re only renting their compute.

At some point, the market might force them to own more of their compute because their own competitors don’t want to lease their capacity to the leading company.

How do you see that playing out?

We definitely see both OpenAI and Anthropic going more direct and not owning the compute, but more rent-to-own, or going through an SPV as some financial sponsors do and producing the compute more directly versus renting.

There are two points to this.

Google, from one perspective, is also selling its external chips to customers and saying, “We don’t care to monetize this within Google Cloud or even allocate the share...

If you think we’re very chip-constrained, we don’t even care that these are going to DeepMind or internal GCP compute for us to monetize.

We’re just willing to become a chip seller.” Anthropic loves TPUs and there are 3.5 to 4 gigawatts-plus, and probably more in the pipeline, in terms of orders there of Anthropic buying these chips directly to then rent.

So yes, the market is good.

Wait, it’s not buying them directly to rent.

So they’re buying them into a neocloud?

Yeah, they buy them through an SPV, or the SPV buys them and then they rent it from the SPV.

Got it.

Okay.

Even within Google Cloud or AWS or Foundry, Anthropic is massive — 48 percent of their business comes through the Bedrock Foundry and Vertex where people are paying through their existing cloud relationship to access these models.

They’re not even talking to Anthropic.

You don’t have to interact with the Anthropic sales force.

You mentioned this earlier.

This marketing channel where Anthropic gets a rev share.

Right.

If you’re AWS and you’re saying, “I’m running Anthropic compute for, let’s say, $10 million per megawatt, but now I’m getting 16 percent of $65 billion-a-megawatt plus the compute costs as well,” so we’re seeing margins at all the clouds go up right now.

Part of it is CPU utilization is going up because of all the coding and then some on the [reinforcement learning] side, but these token-as-a-service businesses as we call them — so AWS Bedrock, Microsoft Foundry, Google Gemini Agent Enterprise platform, which is formerly Vertex — are actually massively increasing the margins on AI at these clouds.

They’re benefiting as well when shareholders are giving them credit for this recently.

In Q2, both Azure and AWS had extremely, extremely strong quarters, AWS specifically, on the back of Anthropic’s growth on Bedrock.

Do you think that will keep Amazon from ever wanting to train its own frontier models?

They’re doing a good job of letting AWS be the infrastructure for everybody else, but they’re one of the only big tech companies that hasn’t felt the insecurity of not having their own models.

Yeah, it’s interesting.

Amazon is very happy to serve a wide variety of customers and they have very little [frontier capability].

When we look at our estimates of training compute, they have the least of any hyperscaler, except maybe Oracle.

It doesn’t seem like there’s much strategy there.

I know Microsoft in the last two quarters has been talking about it a little more.

AWS on the call has been talking about it a little more, but it’s not huge.

They’re not doing it to the same extent that Meta is or trying to be competitive here or even Google with Gemini.

Especially someone like Dylan will tell you, if you’re not trying to compete at the frontier, there’s really not a place for you, especially if you’re only dedicating a few hundred megawatts internally.

One, internal use case is like serving Amazon retail, but then two, training.

There are a lot of commitments to make to be good at this.

It’s a conversation for a different day, but I look at these Microsoft job cuts and I see it as the glimmer of evidence that they’re going to try to compete in the future.

They obviously got burned pretty badly by OpenAI.

Yeah.

They have, in the new agreement that they signed, the right to monetize OpenAI models for essentially not paying OpenAI anything within that agreement.

They’re going to have some interesting things ahead where they monetize the OpenAI models or even through Microsoft 365 Cowork and Copilot applications where they’re not paying OpenAI anything for a frontier model.

The other dynamic here, and you brought it up earlier, is over the last few weeks, there’s just been a lot of stress about neoclouds — whether they will succeed, whether they will fail.

I think Elon Musk said there will be a guppy-like extinction event , which is just a brutal metaphor to use to describe a bunch of data centers.

But this is a bunch of circular financing and Nvidia stood a bunch of them up and maybe the hyperscalers are just going to run away with it.

Maybe Anthropic’s demand, because maybe they will want to own more of their own compute because renting it is precarious in all these ways.

What do you make of the neoclouds?

Do you think they’re going to survive the market actually shaking itself out as these companies go public?

Elon obviously has some incentive to say neoclouds are going to be extinct.

ClusterMAX said something else and just does amazing ratings of the neoclouds .

There are a lot of neoclouds that are ex-crypto miners that are not good businesses and are not good at operating clusters.

I just want to point out CoreWeave is an ex-crypto mining company, right?

Yeah.

I don’t mean CoreWeave, but there are others further down the list.

CoreWeave, Nebius, and anyone that has backing or backstops from one of the major labs, hyperscalers, Nvidia, or Broadcom is going to be okay.

It’s that longer tail.

Hyperscalers have been 65 percent of CapEx and net new compute brought online.

There’s 35 percent of the market that doesn’t have the balance sheets that the hyperscalers have.

Both Google and Meta have recently raised or announced they’re going to raise.

When we look at the big four hyperscalers, they don’t actually need to raise that money over the next two years, even though CapEx is growing from $1.2 to $2 trillion pretty quickly.

But for a lot of these other neoclouds, if you don’t have that sort of backing, I think it is very hard, even right now, and becoming extremely difficult if you don’t have the backing or backstops from those players to keep building compute.

It’s a very, very tough financing market.

One of the things I think is really interesting about Elon in particular talking about neoclouds dying and obviously hyping up his own data center business is he’s trying to put them in space and to get away from the backlash in the United States around data centers in particular.

We have a lot of coverage about data center backlash in the United States, it is slowing down a lot of projects.

But at the rate we’re going, if you think the neoclouds are shaky, you might actually end up abandoning a bunch of GPUs and half-built data centers or have them tied up in financing agreements where they can’t be lit up.

What do you make of that?

Do you think we actually just need to go to space?

Or do you think the market is going to rationalize and actually take advantage of all the compute that is currently allocated but not being used?

We’ll rationalize more so.

The market is very good at finding places to put chips here on the ground.

Politically, we’ll see what happens next week with midterms and the fallout from that.

Obviously, there are some very large sites that still have massive permitting problems.

There’s the entire power equation as we look towards next year.

The data centers will be built.

There will be a method to get these built.

The biggest thing — and the hyperscale CFOs have said this — from an overbuilt perspective and on a relative basis, it’s pretty cheap to build the data center shell.

What they can do if they overbuild is they’re going to say, “We’re just not going to take delivery of the chip.

We’re not going to buy chips.

We’re not going to fill them up.” They’ll just sit empty and chipless.

But the majority of the spend is on the chip side.

So if we do end up in a place where we’re actually oversupplied from a data center perspective, I know that’s a little bit different.

It’s the exact opposite of what the question was.

They have said that from an ROI perspective.

This comes back to that larger question of whether we are still going to be super supply constrained.

A lot of people now, especially in the last three weeks, are talking about, “Are we in this massive glut of compute as we look towards 2028 actually?” Because the same thing we talked about from Anthropic going from negative 94 percent margins to positive 85 percent and compute efficiencies mean as you bring on more inference megawatts that are making a lot more revenue per megawatt, all else SQL, you need less compute.

So it’s a question of whether we we going to have enough revenue in 2028 to justify the ROI on $2 trillion plus of CapEx.

This is why I spent so much time asking about capability overhang and how good the models are today, because you can see some competitor that is less idealistic about AGI saying, “Actually, we’re going to do a bunch of forward-deployed engineers in all of these verticals where they haven’t taken advantage of AI and sell them high-margin inference because we’ll automate big chunks of their business and they’ll see the return.” Right now, a bunch of the Fortune 500 has not seen a return on AI spending .

So if you’re actually just better at customer service and deployment and productizing the model, you might get way ahead of where Anthropic needs to be because they’re still thinking about AGI every single minute of every single day.

I look at Dario standing next to Marc Benioff at Dreamforce and that dude does not want to be there right now.

He wants to be thinking about the machine god.

There’s something there where you can just see competitors coming up with an open source model and saying, “We’re actually going to productize this and we will actually take the revenue that everyone else is depending on.” Yeah, it’s extremely, extremely interesting.

In the interim, that’s why it is getting more verticalized because you need something to bridge AGI where it just fully does the job, you need something to bridge the actual model today. [Laughs] Yeah.

We’ll just take that for granted.

To get there, you need some bridges of where it sits with the actual end user at some point.

Everything is going to come down to this: Is there going to be some timing or adoption mismatch where we just don’t get the revenue at a certain point of time to justify that chase of “train and compute towards AGI”?

That’s a risk.

The other risk we look at is whether we get more models at the frontier even at the open source that are as competitive in coding, where token pricing across the frontier needs to be taken down, because like I mentioned earlier, there are lower switching costs.

Even at SemiAnalysis, we went from 95 percent or 90 percent-plus of our usage at the end of Q2 was on Anthropic’s models down to 70 percent after the release of OpenAI’s ChatGPT 5.6 and Astra.

And then with Opus 5.5, it’s gone back to 90 percent-plus roughly.

It does come back.

Even the base of revenue today — and they’ve said that we have net revenue retention of 900 percent, so they’re seeing this massive, massive growth.

This isn’t a traditional software business like ServiceNow or Workday, where you have just an incredible logo or gross retention of 95 percent to 98 percent and customers sign these nice three-year contracts, they never churn, they add some seats, and maybe they adopt another product that is being upsold.

This is purely consumption.

The other portion was the 20 percent drop in the last two weeks of the year versus the prior two weeks last year in token spend, because of the holiday season.

You’re not going to do work code stuff, you’re not going to be coding for work during the holidays.

This is extremely, extremely pure consumption business, even different from how we think about Snowflake or Datadog today in public markets.

Obviously, Anthropic is not the only company that’s going to have an IPO.

OpenAI is right next to them.

They’ve delayed theirs.

You mentioned earlier Anthropic is much more enterprise focused.

I think OpenAI for a long time thought that Google wouldn’t react to them and they would just take the search business away and everything would be fine.

Google obviously reacted for better or worse.

Search is now AI Overviews.

Looking at the Anthropic S-1, what are you looking ahead to with OpenAI?

Because they are a more consumer facing company.

OpenAI was 60-40 consumer, 60 percent consumer and 40 percent enterprise at the end of Q1.

That didn’t flip for the first time until January or August to be enterprise focused.

What they’ll tell you is enterprise business — because it was so consumer and subscription focused, this consumption business that’s 80 percent of Anthropic’s revenue — didn’t take off until a release of 5.6 and then with Astra.

Those are really great models.

OpenAI took the majority of actual net new ARR in Q3, but it’s going to take some time because what’s been in the Wall Street Journal , like negative 100 percent EBITA margins versus we’re seeing positive 11 percent here.

There are some differences, some pretty big differences, in the business model where they just don’t monetize at the same rate that Anthropic does.

That’s a little bit because the business makeup — the verticals, that consumer-versus-enterprise split — and that’s changing.

What they’ll tell you is they see a really good Q4 and they have a much stronger enterprise sales function than Anthropic has.

I expect them to come up, but I don’t think the financials are going to look as good as this even when they drop their S-1 maybe in early 2027.

Do you think that’s why they delayed it?

To get their financials looking better?

Yeah, I think OpenAI had a really strong Q3 .

Enterprise grew 100 percent quarter-over-quarter versus the total business which was 77 percent.

You get another strong quarter of enterprise here.

If Opus 5.5 didn’t take a ton of share, that would put OpenAI in a much better position to tell the story.

There are some other turns here between now and when Anthropic actually goes public.

They’re going to do a roadshow.

There’ll be some pricing events.

What are you looking for from Anthropic?

They did an investor day two or three weeks ago where they did give some more color.

I think they’ll walk through why Q3 was so weak.

Meta was a very, very large customer, probably over 10 percent.

What’s been publicly reported is they went from 60,000 Claude Code seats down to 30,000.

These token volumes didn’t disappear, they just shifted into Meta’s internal models.

Anthropic started cracking down on anti-distillation, and that was 5 percent of revenue prior.

I think they said 5 percent to 7 percent of revenue in the S-1 and stuff against their terms of service.

So what’s here on the roadshows is a lot of this October acceleration after Opus 5.5.

We believe that they’re back on track.

If they were doing $10 billion of net new ARR per month in Q2 and that fell down to $4 billion in Q3, that they’re getting back on that $8 billion to $10 billion pace here in Q4.

People want to hear about these new verticals, specifically cyber.

They’re doing some patching until they have that full cyber SKU rolled out, but they’re definitely monetizing cyber today for vulnerability code scanning.

These are not small contracts, I should say, with existing customers.

I think they’ll start to message what the 2027 ARR growth path looks like.

The other thing too is expectations management, keeping numbers low enough, not talking about AGI as much. [Laughs] It’s hard to do expectation management when your risk factors are like, “We could pose an existential risk to all of humanity.” [Laughs] Right.

And so saying you do that — you’re going to achieve AGI at some point, you’re going to replace everyone’s jobs — but then trying to keep numbers low enough for Q4 and to have this massive beat the first quarter you become public and have a decent guide for 2027, it’ll be a nice mix of seesawing between that long-term vision and short-term expectations management.

There’s a lot going on.

Joey, this has been great.

We’re going to have to have you back as these companies barrel towards actually being public and their economics become much more visible.

Thank you so much for being on Decoder .

Thank you so much.

I appreciate it.

Questions or comments?

Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com.

We really do read every email!

articles.full_text:
The October inflection point for vibe game development 28th October 2026 I’ve written before about how November 2025 was an inflection point for coding agents —the point where Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.1 crossed a tipping point that meant their respective coding agents became reliable daily drivers for software engineers.

I think we’ve reached a new inflection point in October 2026, and this time it’s for vibe coding computer games .

Tree Appreciator Emberwick Battle Drones Pumpkin Farmer, aka Quarter Sun Cove Four times as insulting What happens if someone actually puts the work in?

You should build a game!

Claude Opus 5.5 in particular exhibits meaningful improvements in several areas needed to build a compelling game: 3D modeling Music generation (see Scrimshaw Jukebox ) Game design (!) That last one is particularly important.

Models have been able to create something that looks like a game for quite a while now, as seen in my previous experiments .

The challenge has been getting to a game that’s actually fun to play .

Game design is a deep subject area.

I won’t pretend to be well versed in it—I know enough to have respect for it as a craft.

Creating a novel, compelling gameplay loop which challenges players at the right level and provides a satisfying learning curve is a fine art.

I didn’t think the models could do it.

Then I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 to “Make it a LOT more fun”... and it did .

In the past few weeks I’ve vibe coded (in the classic sense of the term —no looking at the code at all) four games that I’ve genuinely enjoyed playing.

I attended Foo Camp in Berkeley over the weekend and met several people who were having similar experiences.

Building games that play well is shockingly easy now.

The new challenge is coming up with concepts for games that are novel and delightful and that wouldn’t exist without AI assistance.

I haven’t done an exhaustive study, but my current impression is that GPT-6 Astra isn’t quite there yet.

It can absolutely build a game, but its sense of fun doesn’t match that of Opus 5.5.

I expect OpenAI will get there by the end of the year.

Here are the four game projects that have convinced me that the models are now capable of producing fun games with very little guidance.

All four are built in HTML and JavaScript and run entirely in the browser.

Tree Appreciator The smallest game I found to be genuinely delightful is Tree Appreciator .

I used the regular Claude chat interface for this—it didn’t even need Claude Code.

I built this on a whim while we were driving along Skyline Boulevard looking at trees.

My prompt was: Build a three js game called "Tree appreciator" - it shows you two algorithmically generated trees and the game mechanics is about appreciating the differences between them.

Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful.

I’ve found that telling models to use three.js works really well.

Claude doesn’t have its own image generation model but is capable of building full-color 3D models that look and feel excellent.

This game required no iteration or follow-up prompting at all—I got the game in a single shot.

It gave me back a charming little mobile-friendly spot-the-difference game.

You can play that here .

Here’s the chat transcript that built it.

It’s pleasingly relaxing.

The graphics are fun, and collecting trees that you have completed in a “herbarium” provides a nice, cosy sense of accomplishment.

Emberwick This was a more ambitious project that I again built using regular Claude chat.

I started out by building an experimental prototype of an engine for a top-down fantasy RPG: Build a demo game engine three.js which is a top down (but at an angle) RPG - the player gets to move through the world with one or two companions.

Create a fantasy village setting that demonstrates walking around outside and then shows how when the player enters a building the wall between the player and the camera goes transparent so the user can see what is happening Add some NPCs and plenty of furniture and different types of building some with an upstairs - be creative, make it look great Here’s that first version .

It worked really well!

I was inspired to increase my ambitions: Make it not so flat - the buildings are great but the landscape itself is completely flat at the moment, fix that Add basements to two of the buildings with a tunnel system joining them below the village Add the start of a rocky mountain on one side of the village containing a cave with a sleeping troll Here’s that version .

When that produced a good result, I decided to push it all the way: Now turn this into an actual game - quadruple the size of the playable area, introduce fun game mechanics, add a plot that isn't too cliche, some twists, a magic system, make it really good We’re back to prompts like “make it really good” here!

Asking for a plot that “isn’t too cliche” seemed to work too—it’s a bit cliché, but still novel enough that I enjoyed following the story.

Unlike Tree Appreciator, this took quite a bit of additional playtesting and prompting to get to a finished version.

This was mainly due to gameplay problems—things like a character not being in the right place to complete a quest because a different story element had caused them to move to another location.

Here’s that final game .

It has a full story that takes about 15 minutes to play through.

There’s even an experimental level editor if you want to drop in your own houses, furniture, and landscape features.

Once it was all working (and I’d iterated through some gameplay bugs), I played it through from start to finish and found myself emotionally affected by the ending!

I’m somewhat embarrassed by this, because everything in this game—the graphics, the plot, the characters, the music, the dialog—came from the model.

My creative input was pretty much just “it’s a fantasy village and there’s a troll asleep in a cave”.

Here’s the full shared Claude chat in which I built this game.

I also fed that same initial sequence of prompts through ChatGPT GPT-6 Pro.

Here’s the transcript and the finished game for comparison.

It looks great, but I don’t think it plays nearly as well.

Battle Drones This is by far my most successful project, which I wrote about last week .

It’s a Command & Conquer-style Real-Time Strategy game where two robot armies (or four as of Saturday ) build units, harvest scrap, and battle over territory.

This is also the project that convinced me that Opus 5.5 knows what “fun” is.

The first versions were built back in July using Claude Fable 5.

It got me to a workable 2D Command & Conquer-style game, but it wasn’t great to play.

I prompted Opus 5.5 to “Make it a LOT more fun” and then later to “Port this game to three.js” and the game was transformed.

There’s a blow-by-blow account (prompts included) in my write-up .

Today, Battle Drones has 2-4 player multiplayer (via a vibe coded WebSockets relay server), medals, replays, seven maps, a random map generator, and a set of “mutators” that add variants of the rules.

It also lets different LLMs play against each other, using a mode where the game advances five seconds and then pauses to give different models time to interpret the new game state and line up their next set of commands.

Here’s a replay of Claude Haiku 5.5 vs.

GPT-6 Luna : Battle Drones is a particularly good example of Opus 5.5’s ability to create 3D models.

This page lets you browse all of the models in the game .

I released Battle Drones under the Apache 2.0 License last Tuesday.

On Wednesday Gabriel Turpin released Panache ( screenshots here ), a fork of Battle Drones that reimagined the game for steampunk 1900s Belle Époque France, with new models and music and an animated intro sequence.

Open source at work!

Pumpkin Farmer, aka Quarter Sun Cove I live in Half Moon Bay, California , home of the annual Half Moon Bay Art and Pumpkin Festival , which includes a giant pumpkin weigh-off competition.

I decided to try building a game that wasn’t just a cheap imitation of something that already existed, so I set out to create a game about farming pumpkins, growing giant pumpkins, and handling the rush of the October pumpkin season.

I called it “Quarter Sun Cove”.

I’m still iterating on this project, but it’s shaping up quite nicely.

It’s a cosy farming simulator where you spend the year tending to your giant pumpkin and planting out regular-sized pumpkins for sale in October, then sell pumpkins during pumpkin season and enter your giant pumpkin in the weigh-off.

Every character in it is a (vegetarian) animal.

The mayor of the town is a pelican.

You can be a pelican, skunk, raccoon, possum, beaver, coyote, fox, owl, sea otter, or harbor seal.

Those species all later show up (accompanied by their children) to buy pumpkins from you.

It’s absurdly cute.

You can play the latest version here .

I’m not convinced by the game mechanics yet—it’s actually quite complicated: you have to decide when to plant pumpkins such that they will become ripe at the weekends in October with the most visitors.

Here’s the initial brainstorming session , which resulted in this spec file .

Then I had Opus 5.5 Ultracode burn millions of tokens and nearly two days building it.

I told Claude to “surprise and delight the user frequently” and the result is so many little details and easter eggs.

There are mischievous raccoons, an elephant seal that runs the weigh-off, harbor seals that roll their pumpkins back into the ocean, a wandering goat, and superstitions about growing giant pumpkins that sometimes come true.

This isn’t my best game yet—it’s not as fun to play as Battle Drones—but it represents the kind of game I want more of: weird, fun, uniquely personal—something that wouldn’t have been built in the before-times.

Four times as insulting If you are offended by AI-generated art, AI-generated music, AI-generated writing, and AI-generated code, I have bad news for you: vibe coded games combine all of those at once .

I respect those opinions, even though I don’t strongly hold them myself.

The wider games community already has an aversion to AI-generated assets in games.

This has been a growing issue over the past few years as tools like Midjourney have enabled developers to generate assets for their projects.

This IGN story covering complaints about slop in Valve’s Steam Next Fest is a good recent example.

We now have games where everything —code, assets, dialog, and even the game design itself—can be outsourced to the models.

And the results don’t suck!

Building a computer game used to be one of the most challenging projects in all of software development, combining a diverse range of skills and requiring intense focus and effort over many months or even years.

And now here I am spitting out a playable multiplayer RTS by prompting on my phone!

I expect that, as we’ve already seen with programming, this will result in a split.

Some players will refuse to have anything to do with games that were built in this way.

Others may embrace this as opening up game development to a much wider audience.

I lean in that direction!

I certainly won’t be entering any of my vibe coded games in traditional game jams or competitions—I don’t feel like I’ve earned that right.

We’ll likely see new avenues emerge for vibe game developers to compare their projects.

What happens if someone actually puts the work in?

The thing I find both exciting and shameful about this is that I have got interesting results from so little creative input .

The projects I’ve described here are loosely ordered by how much effort I’ve put into them.

Not a single project represents more than four hours of my work (plus many more hours of Claude Code churning away by itself).

Now imagine what could be achieved by anyone who takes this seriously, invests significant creative time, applies better taste in game design, and then playtests and iterates on the result until it’s as good as they can make it.

I want to see games that wouldn’t have existed without these new tools.

You should build a game!

Building games in this way is so much fun .

It’s the perfect application for vibe coding because it’s so low stakes: how much damage can you cause with a bug in a personal vibe coded game project? (OK, you can do some damage... my attempt at audio-based multiplayer gave my wife Natalie a nasty headache !) All of my games so far have been HTML and JavaScript using static hosting (generally GitHub Pages or Cloudflare Pages).

Modern browsers—including mobile browsers—are incredibly capable.

Frontier models already know libraries like three.js and Phaser .

I’m finding these mobile web games to be indistinguishable from the native experience, at least for the kinds of games I’m trying to build.

I suggest starting with a prompt like this: Build a mobile-friendly three.js game where...

This works on both chatgpt.com and claude.ai —you don’t even need to fire up a full coding agent.

As one last example, here’s “Build a mobile-friendly three.js game where a mouse has to hide from a cat” by Claude Opus 5.5 Extra and by GPT-6 Extra High .

Switch to Codex or Claude Code once your project passes the proof-of-concept phase.

And if the game isn’t fun enough, add this: Make it a LOT more fun

articles.full_text:
29th October 2026 - Link Blog API credits benefit for eligible ChatGPT subscriptions .

Earlier this month Anthropic announced a generous new benefit for their Max and Team subscriptions: $100, $200, and $500 per month subscribers would get the equivalent quantity of (expiring) credits to use with the Anthropic API.

OpenAI have now launched pretty much exactly the same deal: if you have a $100, $200, or $500 subscription plan with them you now get that same quantity of credits to apply to one of your API organizations.

I maintain subscriptions with both companies, so this is great news for me!

I may even ship some public-facing demos now that the credits are already covered by my existing subscriptions.
